summary.title: The Rule of Three
summary.one_liner: Software is only reusable after it has been proven in three different applications or audiences, a rule of thumb Jeff Atwood applies to Stack Overflow and Discourse.
keywords: facts and fallacies of software engineering
how do i know my code is reusable
why software is hard to generalize
takeaways: Building truly reusable software is about three times harder than building single-use components, per the rule from Facts and Fallacies of Software Engineering.
A reusable component should be tried in three different applications or audiences before it is general enough for a reuse library.
One user may be luck, two gives some confidence, and three shows the solution generalizes.
Stack Overflow expanded to Server Fault and Super User to test the engine on three audiences before Stack Exchange grew into a network.
Before calling something reusable, find three users or audiences to validate it.
summary.summary: Jeff Atwood argues that programmers overestimate how general their solutions are and that real reusability is hard. He cites the "rule of three" from Facts and Fallacies of Software Engineering: reusable components cost about three times more to build, and should be tried in three different applications before entering a reuse library. He illustrates the idea with Stack Overflow, Server Fault and Super User, and with the staged partner rollout of Discourse. The post is an informal essay with personal anecdotes rather than a technical tutorial.
